spans.content: Role of Nitrogen in the Pitting Resistance
of Cast Duplex CF-Type Stainless Steels
S. J. Pawel,* E. E. Stansbury,** and C. D. Lundin**
ABSTRACT
In this investigation, critical manipulation, observation, and analy-
sis of polarization curves as a function of nitrogen content in cast
duplex CF-type stainless steels (SSs) has been performed.
These, in conjunction with microstructural observations and
atomic absorption spectroscopic analyses of polarization cell so-
lutions, have led to the discovery of nitrogen's major role in the
corrosion resistance of SSs. Nitrogen has been found to encour-
age the retention of chromium in the passive film and near sur-
face layers during corrosion, which improves pitting resistance.
INTRODUCTION
During the past 10 to 15 years, nitrogen has become an important
alloy addition to many wrought austenitic stainless steels (SSs).
Initially, nitrogen was added as a less costly austenite former than
nickel. An additional motivation for adding nitrogen to SSs results
from the increased use of low-carbon grades of wrought austenitic
SSs in power generation applications, particularly in boiling water
reactor (BWR) and pressurized water reactor (PWR) plant piping.
The use of low-carbon alloys is necessitated by the need to avoid
welding related corrosion problems (i.e., sensitization). Nitrogen
has become a common alloying addition to return the strength of
low-carbon alloys to that of nominal carbon content alloys. During
this material development period, data have accumulated on the
effects of nitrogen additions on corrosion properties of wrought
SSs, strongly suggesting that nitrogen improves intergranular and
pitting corrosion resistance in these steels.1.2
The high-alloy casting industry is adding nitrogen to selected
grades of corrosion-resistant castings in response to the demand
for higher performance alloys and as a consequence of the suc-
cess the wrought alloy industry has had with nitrogen additions.
Unfortunately, there is a small amount of data on nitrogen effects
on the corrosion behavior of high-alloy duplex cast materials. In
response, research was initiated to document the magnitude of the
improvement in localized corrosion resistance resulting from nitro-
gen additions in cast duplex SSs and to elucidate the mechanism
by which this improvement occurs. This paper describes some of
the results regarding the pitting resistance of solution treated CF-
type alloys. CF-type alloys are the cast equivalent of AISI(1)304
SSs; the major difference is that CF alloys generally contain 5 to
25% ferrite in the microstructure, while AISI 304 SS is nominally
fully austenitic.

and austenite-forming elements in duplex SSs (see, for example
the Schoefer diagram),³ it is impossible to vary the concentration

positional variable by making alloys with fixed Cr, Mo, and C con-
tents and decreasing the nickel content as the amount of nitrogen
is increased to maintain approximately constant ferrite.

cast into cylindrical shapes of a size convenient for remelting in a

Atomic Absorption Spectroscopy
The analysis of a polarization curve yields information such
as the relative ability of an alloy to passivate or its susceptibility to
pitting corrosion. The CD value that is determined at any potential
represents the net current at the sample surface and no informa-
tion concerning the ionic composition of this current is available
from the polarization curve. To obtain information on the distribu-
tion of ionic species responsible for the anodic current, chemical
analysis of the test solution following a polarization experiment
must be performed. In this investigation, chemical analyses of test
solutions were performed using atomic absorption spectrometry
(AAS). A Perkin-Elmer(³) Zeeman/3030 system, comprising spec-
trometer, Zeeman graphite furnace unit, and auto-sampler, was
used for all AAS determinations.
Samples were potentiostatically etched in the pitting test solu-
tion at potentials near that of the maximum anodic dissolution CD
and at a potential just greater than that necessary to induce pas-
sivity
( + 2 5 0 \mathsf { m V } _ { \mathsf { s H E } } )
. During dissolution, the CD as a function of
time was recorded so that the total amount of charge transferred
could be calculated. The concentration of each of the major alloy-
ing elements (Fe, Cr, Ni, and Mo) in each test solution, normalized
to unit charge transferred, was then determined and related to the
bulk composition of the alloy in question.
Determination of the contribution of the major alloying ele-
ments to the dissolution current yields important information about
the dissolution process as a function of alloy content, but it also
indirectly yields information about the surface (passive film and
near-surface bulk alloy) composition of the alloy. For example,
other factors such as dissolution potential and test environment
being equal, a test solution that is determined to have a very low
chromium concentration (compared to that following testing of a
different alloy) indicates that the corresponding alloy must have a
surface relatively rich in chromium. This follows because the chro-
mium must be located in the alloy (unoxidized state), in the pas-
sive film (oxidized state), or in the test solution. Such information
may be used in much the same way (qualitatively) as information
obtained from surface analysis techniques.

Major evidence that the low potential loop represents the en-
richment of chromium in the surface layers of the alloy was ob-
tained by analyses of the corrosion products in the test solution
following various dissolution procedures at potentials near the an-
odic loop(s). The analysis of the corrosion products was performed
using atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS). This technique, us-
ing high-temperature graphite furnace technology to vaporize atom
species, enabled reproducible measurements of Fe, Cr, Ni, and
Mo concentrations in the parts per billion (ppb) range to be per-
formed on the polarization cell aqueous environment.
Samples prepared in the standard way were potentiostatically
held at the selected potential (or rapidly scanned to this potential)
for sufficient time to collect a measurable amount of corrosion
products in the 1.8-L test solution. During dissolution, the current
was continually recorded as a function of time so that the total dis-
solution charge could be calculated. The concentrations of Fe, Cr,
Ni, and Mo in the solution were then determined and normalized
to unit dissolution charge. These concentrations were then con-
verted to a percentage of the corrosion product (assuming the
contribution from all other elements is negligible). The percentage
of the corrosion product assigned to each element may then be
related to the percentage of the respective element in the bulk al-
loy. When the ratio (percentage in corrosion products divided by
percentage in the bulk alloy) is less than one, the particular ele-
ment is not going into solution in amounts as great as its presence
in the bulk alloy and is therefore being enriched on the sample
surface and/or in the passive film.

tion, and analysis of cyclic polarization curves as a function of ni-

surface layers) of the nitrogen-containing alloys. Thus, in the pres-
ence of solid solution nitrogen, the surface chromium content of
the alloy is effectively increased and the pitting resistance is ob-
served to improve. The observed trend of the nitrogen effect on
chromium accumulation was observed at al dissolution potentials
examined, but this effect was greatest for active dissolution at po-
tentials near that of the low potential loop.

It is suggested that the completion of an anodic loop potential
scan is not necessary to develop pitting resistance resulting from
nitrogen additions. During the initial burst of current associated
with a pit embryo, active dissolution conditions exist. In the pres-
ence of nitrogen, this current burst contains predominantly iron
ions and the pit surface remaining becomes relatively enriched in
chromium and thus may repassivate more easily than in the ab-
sence of nitrogen. This was observed experimentally in the cyclic
polarization curves for CF alloys. In the passive potential region
(below the pitting potential), the high-nitrogen alloys exhibit much
smaller (and fewer) current excursions than the low-nitrogen alloys
prior to the onset of stable pitting. In addition, the high-nitrogen
alloys were observed to exhibit some tendency toward partial re-
passivation at potentials above that determined to be the pitting
potential.
Finally, it is proposed that, on an atomic scale, the affinity of
nitrogen for chromium discourages chromium dissolution resulting
from a clustering type of effect. Although the clustering-type mech-
anism was not analytically proven, this concept is consistent with
other observations noted in the literature, such as the facts that
nitrogen retards chromium diffusion in the austenite and that nitro-
gen accumulates at the metal/oxide interface of SSs during corro-
sion.
